title: A Security Pro Hacked North Korean Hackers. He Found They’d Breached Hundreds of Networks Worldwide
gist: Security researcher Vangelis Stykas infiltrated North Korean hacking infrastructure for 22 months and found evidence that 1,640 companies across 57 countries were impacted, with 700-800 suffering 'really damaging' root-level intrusions, revealing that the fake-job-offer 'Contagious Interview' technique has quietly compromised far more corporate and crypto infrastructure than publicly known.

themes.theme: Scale of North Korean corporate infiltration

insights.claim: Greece-based researcher Vangelis Stykas gained access to North Korean hacker command-and-control systems roughly 22 months ago and found evidence that 1,640 companies across 57 countries have been impacted by North Korea's hacking operations, with around 700 to 800 of those suffering 'really damaging' intrusions.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: The publicly known North Korean crypto-theft/hacking incidents represent a fraction of true exposure; enterprises and crypto firms should assume higher baseline compromise risk from DPRK-linked contractor infiltration than headline incident counts suggest.
insights.locator: Since Greece-based cybersecurity researcher Vangelis Stykas

insights.claim: Stykas described the access obtained by North Korean hackers in breached organizations as company-wide, including root access to servers and to Amazon Web Services, and for crypto companies, access to private keys and blockchain infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Vangelis Stykas
insights.so_what: Root/AWS-level access at hundreds of firms means the realistic worst case for affected companies is far beyond data exposure — it is full infrastructure and crypto-key compromise; due diligence on vendors and contractors should weight this risk heavily.
insights.quote: It's company access, it's root access to servers, it's root access to AWS. For crypto companies, it's keys, it's blockchain access—it's ridiculous access.
insights.locator: It's company access, it's root access to servers

insights.claim: Stykas says the North Korean hackers in some cases infected themselves with their own malware, which inadvertently gave him access to their Slack, Discord, and workstations, amounting to roughly 5 terabytes of data he has reviewed.
insights.speaker: Vangelis Stykas
insights.so_what: An unusual operational-security failure by the threat actor created a rare, large-scale intelligence window into DPRK hacking tradecraft — a data source likely to inform future threat-intel reporting and defensive playbooks.
insights.quote: I have access to their Slack, I have access to their Discord, I have access to a lot of stuff.
insights.locator: In some cases, he notes, the hackers appeared to have infected themselves

insights.claim: Named companies impacted include Boston Children's Hospital (which held a large Covid-19 database of Americans' personal health data), Japanese tech firm AEON Smart Technology, Chinese phone maker Oppo, crypto firms Coinbase and Uniswap Labs, Italy's Supreme Judicial Council, a subsidiary of Saudi Arabia's Al Rajhi Bank, and Digitaal Vlaanderen (part of the Flemish government in Belgium).
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: These are only the roughly dozen firms Stykas is naming publicly (chosen because they handled disclosure well) out of 700-800 seriously breached organizations — implying many more, unnamed, seriously compromised firms exist across sectors including crypto exchanges and DeFi protocols.
insights.locator: The researcher says these include the Boston Children's Hospital

insights.claim: Nearly all of the affected organizations were compromised via a well-documented tactic in which North Korean hackers lure software developers with fake job offers and high salaries, then ask candidates to download a coding-test program that silently installs malware — a campaign known as Contagious Interview, active since as early as 2022 according to Microsoft.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Companies using external developer contractors should treat fake-recruiter/coding-test lures as an established, still-active attack vector — a cheap, scalable entry point that continues to yield company-wide compromises years after first documented.
insights.locator: In the cases of almost all of the hundreds of hacked firms

insights.claim: Stykas found that compromised external contractors, who often held developer keys and multi-system access, vastly increased the blast radius of successful attacks, with some individual contractors having access to up to 30 different companies.
insights.speaker: Vangelis Stykas
insights.so_what: A single compromised or fraudulent contractor can function as a pivot point into dozens of companies simultaneously, making contractor vetting and access segmentation a high-leverage security control.
insights.quote: I have seen a couple of contractors that had access to up to 30 companies.
insights.locator: For many of the impacted organizations

insights.claim: According to a Dtex cybersecurity report cited in the article, North Korea likely fields several hundred skilled cyber operators trained from a young age, plus 'several thousand' fraudulent remote IT workers embedded at legitimate companies, both groups working under yearly earnings quotas set by the regime.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: This is an industrialized, quota-driven state operation rather than opportunistic crime, implying persistent and scaling threat volume that companies should budget for as a recurring cost of doing business, not a one-time incident.
insights.locator: North Korea's cyber operations are both sprawling and fluid

insights.claim: Threat intelligence researcher Marcus Hutchins of Expel says North Korean hacking teams tend to stay narrowly focused on stealing crypto wallets even when they have access to more sensitive data, but warns that persistent access could be handed off to separate espionage teams within North Korea's operation.
insights.speaker: Marcus Hutchins (via Matt Burgess)
insights.so_what: Even organizations that see no sign of data misuse beyond crypto theft should not assume they are safe — persistent unauthorized access is a standing risk for follow-on espionage operations, not just financial theft.
insights.quote: It seems like the teams tend to stick to their task of getting crypto wallets. But there's obviously the risk that if they're maintaining persistent access to a corporation, one of the espionage teams could then piggyback off that access.
insights.locator: Hutchins says he's also seen a similar laser focus

themes.theme: Corporate incident response quality varies widely

insights.claim: Coinbase says it investigated a contractor found to be based in the US and found no evidence he was located in North Korea or affiliated with the DPRK government, but its security controls flagged risks suggesting possible unauthorized outsourcing, leading it to terminate the contractor within 30 days of onboarding, before Stykas's tip.
insights.speaker: Coinbase spokesperson (via Matt Burgess)
insights.so_what: Illustrates that internal security controls can catch outsourcing/subcontracting red flags even without confirming DPRK nexus — a useful detection pattern (anomalous technology setup suggesting a hidden subcontractor) for other firms screening contractors.

insights.claim: The Flemish government's Digitaal Vlaanderen confirmed it was notified of the incident via Belgium's national cybersecurity center on March 3, 2026 and says it isolated the affected workstation and revoked and rotated the exposed credentials and access, describing the incident as contained and remediated.
insights.speaker: Flemish government spokesperson (via Matt Burgess)
insights.so_what: A concrete example of a fast, structured remediation playbook (isolate device, revoke/rotate credentials) following third-party disclosure, useful as a benchmark for incident response speed.
insights.locator: We can confirm that we were notified of this incident

insights.claim: Stykas says the real concern is not the roughly dozen companies he is naming publicly (chosen because they handled disclosure well) but the hundreds of organizations that never responded to his warnings, with more being added to the list every day; what began as his side project is now his full-time job.
insights.speaker: Vangelis Stykas
insights.so_what: Signals an ongoing, expanding compromise surface with most affected companies still unaware or unresponsive — the disclosed dozen names are the tip of a much larger, largely unremediated iceberg.
insights.quote: This started as a side project, and right now it's my full-time job.
insights.locator: Given the danger of those breaches

insights.claim: Stykas argues that how a company responds to being hacked, not whether it gets hacked, is what separates good companies from bad ones, and says many companies he has dealt with have responded poorly.
insights.speaker: Vangelis Stykas
insights.so_what: Reinforces that incident-response maturity, not breach avoidance, is becoming the differentiator investors and partners should assess when evaluating a company's cybersecurity posture.
insights.quote: They're here, they're hacking us nonstop. At the end of the day, everyone's getting hacked. How you treat you being hacked is what separates a good company from a bad company. And we have seen a lot of bad companies.
insights.locator: They're here, they're hacking us nonstop
